vignette:
Ravi, 41, finds himself staring at a blank canvas on his screen, the cursor blinking mockingly. He’s a graphic designer, usually quick with ideas, a master of vibrant palettes and precise layouts. But lately, his mind feels like a grey, static-filled screen. His wife, Priya, often finds him lost in thought, a distant look in his eyes, even when they’re sharing a meal. He’s always been reserved, but this new quietness is different; it’s heavy, laden with an unspoken burden.

The burden began nearly a year ago, on a crisp autumn evening. He was driving home from a late work session, a new client brief buzzing in his head. He’d stopped at a traffic light, minding his business, when the flashing blue and red lights filled his rearview mirror. Two officers approached his car, their faces stern, their hands hovering near their belts. They said his car matched the description of one involved in an incident. Ravi, confused and a little annoyed, tried to explain. But their tone hardened. He was asked to step out, hands on the roof. The cold metal of handcuffs bit into his wrists, the suddenness of it all a shock. He remembers the feeling of his heart hammering against his ribs, the humiliation as passersby glanced, the burning shame of being paraded as a suspect when he had done nothing wrong. He was taken to the station, interrogated for hours, the air thick with suspicion and an underlying current he couldn't quite name – a feeling of being judged before he even spoke. Eventually, they realized their mistake, a mix-up with a similar make and model, and he was released with a curt apology that felt utterly hollow.

In the initial days, a furious anger simmered beneath his skin. He wanted to rail against the injustice, to demand accountability, but a deep-seated fear held him back. He tried to brush it off, to tell himself it was a one-off incident, but the images kept flashing back: the blinding headlights, the glint of the badge, the cold steel on his wrists. Sleep became a battleground. He’d wake up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, from vivid nightmares of being chased, of being trapped in a sterile interrogation room with no way out.

He started avoiding the route home that night, taking long detours that added twenty minutes to his commute. The sight of a police cruiser, even in the distance, sends a jolt of anxiety through him, his muscles tensing, his breath catching. He finds himself constantly scanning his surroundings, especially when he’s out in public, looking for potential threats, for anyone in uniform. This hypervigilance bleeds into his home life. A sudden loud noise makes him jump; Priya’s gentle touch sometimes startles him.

At work, his once sharp focus has dulled. He struggles to concentrate on the intricate details of a logo, his mind drifting to the memory of the cold metal on his skin. Creativity, his lifeblood, feels sapped. He often misses deadlines, leading to frustrated clients and a growing sense of inadequacy. He pours hours into mundane tasks, anything to avoid the more demanding creative work, but even then, his thoughts are often hijacked. He finds himself designing stark, almost sterile images, devoid of the warmth and energy that once characterized his portfolio. He can spend an entire day staring at his screen, meticulously adjusting pixels, not because it's necessary, but because the repetitive motion provides a fleeting distraction from the internal turmoil.

Priya tries to reach him, her soft questions about his day met with short, evasive answers. He feels a wall growing between them, a barrier he can’t articulate. He loves her deeply, but the trauma has left him feeling numb, detached, especially from moments of joy or intimacy. He feels a profound sense of shame, as if the incident somehow diminished him, made him less of a man. The world no longer feels safe, and he carries that heavy burden alone, constantly braced for something bad to happen, forever reliving the moment his sense of security was shattered by the flash of blue and red.
